verses.text: When David and his men reached Ziklag on the third day, they found the Amalekites had raided the south and attacked and burned Ziklag.
They had taken the women and everyone else captive, young and old. They hadn't killed anyone. They carried them off and went on their way.
David and his men found the city burned down, and their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
David and his men cried out and wept until they had no strength left to cry.
Both of David's wives had been taken captive: Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail from Carmel, Nabal's widow.
David was in deep distress. The men talked about stoning him because they were grieving for their sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
David told Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech's son, “Please bring me the ephod.” Abiathar brought it to him.
David asked the LORD, “If I go after these raiders, will I catch them?” The LORD answered, “Go after them. You'll catch them and recover everything.”
David set out with his six hundred men. They reached the Besor Brook, where some of the men stayed behind.
David kept going with four hundred men. The other two hundred were too exhausted to cross the brook and stayed there.
The men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him bread to eat and water to drink.
They also gave him part of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. After eating, he revived. He hadn't eaten or drunk anything for three days and three nights.
David asked, “Who do you belong to? Where are you from?” He answered, “I'm a young Egyptian, a servant of an Amalekite. My master left me when I got sick three days ago.
We raided the southern lands of the Cherethites, Judah, and Caleb, and burned Ziklag.”
David asked, “Will you take me to the raiders?” He answered, “Swear by God you won't kill me or hand me back to my master, and I'll take you to them.”
When the Egyptian led David there, the raiders were spread out across the ground, eating, drinking, and dancing over all the goods they'd taken from Philistine territory and Judah.
David fought them from twilight until the following evening. Only four hundred young men escaped, fleeing on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing was missing, small or large, sons or daughters, goods or anything else the raiders had taken. David brought everything back.
David took all the flocks and herds. His men drove them ahead of their own livestock and said, “This is David's plunder.”
David came back to the two hundred men who'd been too exhausted to follow him and had stayed at the Besor Brook. They came out to meet David and his men, and David greeted them.
Some wicked men who'd gone with David said, “They didn't go with us, so they get none of the plunder we recovered. Each man can take his own wife and children and leave.”
David answered, “Don't do that, my brothers. The LORD gave us all this. He kept us safe and handed over the raiders who came against us.
Who would agree with you? The men who guard the supplies get the same share as the men who go into battle. They'll share equally.”
From that day forward David made it a law and rule for Israel, and it still stands today.
When David reached Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends among Judah's elders. “Here's a gift for you from what was taken from the LORD's enemies.”
He sent gifts to the people in Bethel, Ramoth in the south, and Jattir,
to the people in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa,
to the people in Racal and the towns of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites,
to those in Hormah, Borashan, and Athach,
and to Hebron and every other place where David and his men had stayed.
